title: The Mudal Āzhwārs
body:
Poigai Āzhwār

Tondai Nāḍu, a land renowned for its radiance and natural beauty, holds many cities, and among them Kanchipuram is said to be especially blessed with wealth and loveliness. Tiru Atthiyūr, known today as Chinna Kanchipuram, lies within it, surrounded by numerous temples of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and so this part of the city is called Vishṇu Kanchi. The larger part, filled with temples of Lord Śiva, is called Śiva Kanchi.

In Vishṇu Kanchi stands Tiruvekhā, also known as the Yathōthakāri Sannidhi, a kshethram with its own special glory and the abundant anugraham of Sriman Nārāyaṇa. Near the Yathōthakāri temple lies a poigai, a small pond filled with fresh and beautiful lotus flowers, and close beside it, Sonna Vaṇṇam Seitha Perumāl gives His sevai to the whole world.

This pond, set within so great a kshethram, has a glory beyond its fragrance and beauty. In the year Siddhārthi, in the month of Aippasi, on Śukla Ashṭami, a Tuesday, under the Tiruvōṇam nakshatram, Poigai Āzhwār was born in it as an amśam of the Lord's sacred conch, the Pāñcajanya, one of the five divine weapons of Emperumān. Because he was born in the poigai, he came to be called Poigai Āzhwār.

From childhood his thoughts were fixed on Sriman Nārāyaṇa alone. He resolved to follow the Lord and to spread His glory throughout the world. He learned the teachings of the Vaishṇavas, lived by them, and led his life as a true Vaishṇava should. Knowing the greatness of devotion to the Lord of Tirumalai, and wishing that His fame should reach every person in the world, he renounced the ordinary attachments of human life: desire, anger and the pursuit of wealth.

Bhūthath Āzhwār

On the shore of the sea in Tondai Nāḍu lies the town of Kaḍal Mallai, a kshethram where devotees who praise Emperumān have always gathered in great numbers.

Kaḍal Mallai is also known as Māmallapuram, and over the years it has come to be called Mahābalipuram. It was named Māmallapuram after Māmallan, a great king of the Pallava dynasty who ruled it. It is called Mahābalipuram after Mahābali Chakravarthi. When Sriman Nārāyaṇa came to him as Vāmana and asked for three paces of land, Mahābali, unable to offer the third, surrendered his own head to receive it. For this complete surrender to Emperumān, Mahābali was blessed with moksham, and the town still carries his name.

Emperumān reveals Himself in different postures in different kshethrams: standing in some (nindra thirukkōlam), seated in others (vīṭrirundha thirukkōlam), and reclining in yet others (kiḍantha thirukkōlam). Kaḍal Mallai is one of the greatest of the kshethrams where the Lord, as Sthala Śayana Perumāl, reclines in kiḍantha thirukkōlam.

To all these glories, the kshethram adds one more. In the year Siddhārthi, in the month of Aippasi, on Navami, under the Aviṭṭam nakshatram, Bhūthath Āzhwār was born in a small mādhavi flower, as an amśam of the Kaumōdakī, the mace of Emperumān and another of His five divine weapons.

From childhood his heart and every thought were turned towards Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and he spent his life singing the Lord's glory.

Pey Āzhwār

According to tradition, Pey Āzhwār was found in a lily in the pond of the Ādi Keśava Perumāl temple in Mylāpūr. In Tamizh, "pey" refers to one who is possessed, and the saint was given this name because he was so utterly, so madly, drawn to the Lord.

The Sri Ādi Keśava Perumāl temple, among the best known temples of Mylāpūr, has a small pond where flowers of many kinds bloom. There, in the year Siddhārthi, in the month of Aippasi, on Daśami, a Thursday, under the Sadhayam nakshatram, Pey Āzhwār was born as a small child in an alli flower, around the seventh century, as an amśam of the Nandakam, the sword of Sriman Nārāyaṇa.

The Night at Tirukkōvalūr

The first three Āzhwārs, Poigai Āzhwār, Bhūthath Āzhwār and Pey Āzhwār, each came to Tirukkōvalūr on the same rainy night. The first to arrive was Poigai Āzhwār of Kanchipuram, who sought shelter for the night at the āśramam of Mṛkaṇḍu Ṛshi. He was given a narrow space, large enough for only one person to lie down, and was told that he was welcome to rest there for the night.

Bhūthath Āzhwār of Māmallapuram arrived soon after and asked for shelter as well. Poigai Āzhwār welcomed him in, saying that where there was room for one to lie down, there was room for two to sit.

Then Pey Āzhwār of Mylāpūr reached the āśramam. He was told that where there was room for one to lie down and two to sit, there was room for three to stand. This is remembered in the saying:

"Oruvar paḍukka, iruvar irukka, mūvar nirkalām."

And so the three stood together through the night, sharing their experiences of the Lord.

A little later, the three Āzhwārs felt the presence of a fourth person among them. With space for only three to stand, they were pressed close together and grew uneasy. Then, through their divine vision, they realised that the fourth was none other than Sriman Nārāyaṇa Himself. Overjoyed, they poured out their praise of the Lord.

Tirukkōvalūr is thus the first kshethram where the first three Āzhwārs sang Pāsurams in praise of the Lord, verses that later came to form part of the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham.

It is believed that the āśramam where the three Āzhwārs stood that rainy night is the very place where the sanctum stands today, and the first three Āzhwārs are honoured within the sanctum itself.
